query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys in the form of nanoscale thin films or lithographically patterned nanoribbons, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles, given that the notable response reported for bulk forms may not persist in a genuinely low-dimensional state and that heat-transfer rate limits cycle frequency? Specify one controlled intervention, predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, applicable operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Relieving intrinsic nanoscale strain via a controlled post‐deposition annealing treatment will reduce magnetoelastic pinning at grain boundaries and interfaces in as‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA thin films/nanoribbons, thereby decreasing magnetic hysteresis and modulating the magnetocaloric response during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloy thin films or lithographically patterned nanoribbons with inherent nanoscale strain and defect-induced magnetic pinning.
generation.intervention: A controlled post-deposition annealing process at moderate temperatures designed to relieve localized strain without causing significant grain growth or phase transformations.
generation.conditions: Low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles under operational temperatures and time scales that highlight the heat-transfer rate limits typical in nanoscale systems.
generation.structural_mediator: Residual strain and defect-induced grain boundary and interfacial roughness acting as pinning sites that mediate magnetoelastic coupling.
generation.mechanism: Annealing reduces local strain and relaxes disordered regions, which in turn diminishes magnetoelastic coupling that pins domain walls. This alteration allows for more reversible domain reorientation under low fields, leading to reduced hysteresis and a modified magnetocaloric effect that is sensitive to heat-transfer limitations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited baseline, annealed films will exhibit lower magnetic hysteresis (narrower magnetization loops) and a shifted magnetocaloric temperature change (ΔT), reflecting a more efficient and reversible magnetization process under cycle conditions that are limited by heat transfer.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited state characterized by intrinsic nanoscale strain and associated magnetic domain pinning causing pronounced hysteresis and a bulk-like magnetocaloric response that may weaken in low-dimensional configurations.
generation.boundary: Observations are expected to hold under low-applied-field conditions (typical of magnetic-cooling cycles) and within the nanoscale (thin film/nanoribbon) regime where heat-transfer rate limits are significant.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the hysteresis reduction and the degree to which the magnetocaloric effect changes remain uncertain, as they may also be influenced by additional confinement effects and interfacial phenomena not solely attributable to strain relaxation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set remains as-deposited, while the other undergoes controlled post-deposition annealing. Subject both sets to identical low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles while monitoring magnetic and thermal responses. Use structural characterization (e.g., XRD, TEM) to verify strain reduction in annealed samples.
measurements: Hysteresis loop measurements via vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM) to assess coercivity and loop area.
Direct measurements of the magnetocaloric temperature change (ΔT) during cyclic magnetic field application.
Structural analysis using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to quantify strain and grain boundary features.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not display a statistically significant reduction in magnetic hysteresis and any measurable shift in the magnetocaloric temperature change (ΔT) relative to the as-deposited baseline, or if structural analysis does not confirm reduced strain, then the hypothesized role of strain-mediated magnetoelastic coupling in governing the magnetocaloric response would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: We have investigated the dielectric and magnetic properties of a thin film of a magnetic high entropy oxide (Nd‐HEO) perovskite that contains five different magnetic transition metal ions and exhibits a static magnetic order below Tmag = 190 K. The dielectric function of the Nd‐HEO layer has been determined as a function of frequency, temperature and applied DC‐electric field, by measuring the capacitance of a serial circuit of inversely stacked Pt/Nd‐HEO/Nb:STO and Nb:STO/Nd‐HEO/Pt capacitor structures. The development of a bulk magnetic order below Tmag = 190 K has been established with DC magnetization and low‐energy muon‐spin‐rotation (LEM) measurements. At T>>Tmag , we observed a rather strong dielectric response with a Debye‐type frequency dependence and a sizeable zero‐frequency constant of ε′r ∼ 230–250 similar to previous reports on epitaxial thin films of non‐magnetic HEO perovskites []. This aligns with the observation that the disorder due to randomly distributed cations helps to soften the oxygen sublattice and thus to increase its polarizability [, , , , , , , , , , , ]. AbstractHigh-entropy alloys could provide a solution for corrosion resistance due to their impressive properties. Solid-state processing of high purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni and Mo metallic powders and consolidation resulted in a bulk material that was further machined into electro spark deposition electrodes. After the stainless steel substrate surface preparation, thin successive layers of the high-entropy alloy were deposited and Pull-Off testing was performed on the newly obtained coating, for a better understanding of the adhesion efficiency of this technique. Good adhesion of the coating to the substrate was proved by the test and no cracks or exfoliations were present. Corrosion resistance testing was performed in a liquid solution of 3.5 wt.% NaCl for 6 h at room temperature and the results obtained validated our hypothesis that CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloys could provide corrosion resistance when coating a stainless steel substrate.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, coatings, adhesion

Traditional soft magnetic bulk alloys are unsuitable for high‐frequency applications, because of their low magnetic conductivity at gigahertz (GHz) frequencies band and large eddy‐current losses.[  ] In comparison, soft magnetic thin films possess unique advantages of low magnetic losses, high cutoff frequencies, and permeability that originate from their remarkable electrical resistivities (ρ) and moderate anisotropic fields.[ ,  ] Further, soft magnetic high‐entropy alloy thin films (HEATFs) exhibit electrical resistivities that are superior to those of the other soft magnetic thin films. For instance, the ρ value of the Co65Ni12Fe23 film is only 21 µΩ·cm,[  ] while that of the Al0.7CoCrFeNi film can reach up to 540 µΩ·cm.[  ] Notably, high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) and HEATFs exhibit remarkable thermal stabilities, corrosion resistances, and robust mechanical properties.[  –  ] Thus, HEATFs are expected to broaden the composition range of the existing soft magnetic films.
